title: NASA gets five seconds of weightlessness by dropping experiments down a shaft

cover.alt: Seen from above, a white experiment capsule sinks into a cart filled with white polystyrene beads, which spray outwards.
cover.credit: NASA Glenn Research Center · Public domain

body: Under NASA's Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, a concrete-lined shaft runs 510 feet (155 m) into the ground. Inside it stands a steel vacuum chamber 470 feet (143 m) tall. Before a drop, almost all the air is pumped out, so nothing slows the falling experiment: for about **5.15 seconds** it and everything inside it fall together, in the same near-weightlessness astronauts feel in orbit. That lets engineers watch how flames, liquids and gases behave in microgravity. The fall ends in a cart of expanded polystyrene beads.

slides.alt: A camera looking down a long round shaft watches a lit experiment package shrink as it falls, then cameras at the bottom show it plunging into a cart of white beads that burst outwards.
slides.caption: Zero Gravity Research Facility, Cleveland: an experiment package falls away down the vacuum chamber, then plunges into a cart of polystyrene beads.
slides.credit: NASA Glenn Research Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.question: The vacuum chamber is 143 m tall. Roughly how many seconds of free fall does a drop give?
slides.explanation: About 5.15 seconds. Falling bodies speed up as they go, so even a drop of well over 100 m is over in about five seconds.

slides.label: air pressure left in the chamber before a drop
slides.text: About 0.013% of normal air pressure at sea level, so air barely drags on the package as it falls.

slides.heading: Stopping is the rough part
slides.note: Deceleration in the bead-filled cart; experiments can weigh up to 2,500 lb (1,130 kg)

slides.heading: Built for rocket fuel
slides.text: The facility was built in 1966 for the Centaur upper-stage rocket. To fire the engines reliably in space, NASA needed to know how liquid fuels behave when they weigh almost nothing. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1985.

slides.question: What stops the falling package at the bottom of the shaft?
slides.explanation: It lands in a deceleration cart filled with expanded polystyrene beads, usually at about 32 g.
